question: What timeframe typically defines an immediate drug reaction after administration?

options.D: Within minutes to a few hours

explanation: Immediate reactions manifest rapidly after exposure, often within minutes to a few hours. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T4#GNS215_U5_T4_h1)

question: Why must nurses watch patients closely right after giving medications?

options.A: To ensure patients swallow pills without water
options.B: To document exact drug manufacturing lot numbers
options.C: To prevent sudden and life-threatening body collapse
options.D: To calculate daily fluid balance accurately

explanation: Immediate drug reactions can escalate quickly, requiring instant nursing intervention to prevent severe harm. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T4#GNS215_U5_T4_h1)

question: Which antibody is mainly responsible for Type I immediate allergic reactions?
explanation: Type I hypersensitivity reactions are driven by IgE antibodies bound to mast cells and basophils. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T4#GNS215_U5_T4_h2)

question: What happens in the body when histamine is released during an acute drug reaction?

options.A: Widespread narrowing of peripheral blood vessels
options.B: Blood vessels widen and leak fluid into tissues
options.C: Immediate stopping of smooth muscle activity
options.D: Total block of all inflammatory pathways

explanation: Histamine causes blood vessels to dilate and leak fluid into tissues, leading to swelling and low blood pressure. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T4#GNS215_U5_T4_h2)

question: A patient has only a mild rash and slight itching after taking a drug. How is this reaction classified?
explanation: Localized skin symptoms without systemic involvement are classified as mild drug reactions. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T4#GNS215_U5_T4_h3)

question: Which clinical sign turns a mild drug reaction into a severe emergency?

options.A: Itching only on the spot where the injection was given
options.B: Trouble breathing and dangerous drop in blood pressure
options.C: A mild rash appearing twenty-four hours later
options.D: Slight stomach upset with normal vital signs

explanation: Shock and compromised airways indicate severe systemic failure requiring emergency intervention. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T4#GNS215_U5_T4_h3)

question: What happens to a patient's blood pressure during severe anaphylactic shock?
explanation: Widespread vasodilation causes a sharp drop in blood pressure during anaphylaxis. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T4#GNS215_U5_T4_h4)

question: A patient getting penicillin starts wheezing, has swollen lips, and feels dizzy. What is likely happening?

options.A: A normal side effect of antibiotics
options.B: A severe allergic reaction affecting the whole body
options.C: A delayed skin reaction to the drug
options.D: Irritation right at the needle insertion spot

explanation: Simultaneous respiratory, skin, and cardiovascular symptoms point directly to systemic anaphylaxis. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T4#GNS215_U5_T4_h4)

question: What is the very first thing a nurse should do if an acute drug reaction starts?

options.B: Leave the bedside to call a doctor
options.D: Write down what is happening in the patient's chart

explanation: Halting further administration of the causative agent stops ongoing systemic exposure. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T4#GNS215_U5_T4_h5)

question: Why should the nurse keep the intravenous line open with normal saline after stopping the trigger drug?

options.A: To measure urine output through a catheter
options.B: To have a ready line for emergency fluids and medications
options.C: To wash out the mouth before giving oxygen
options.D: To dilute any remaining medicine in the stomach

explanation: An open IV line allows rapid administration of emergency medications and intravenous fluids for blood pressure support. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T4#GNS215_U5_T4_h5)

question: How often should you check vital signs during an active, severe drug reaction?

options.A: Once every four hours as per routine
options.B: Once a day during morning handover
options.C: Only after the emergency drugs have finished working
options.D: Every few minutes until the patient is stable

explanation: Frequent interval tracking is essential to catch sudden hemodynamic shifts during acute reactions. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T4#GNS215_U5_T4_h6)

question: What does a fast heart rate and falling oxygen level mean during a drug reaction?

options.A: The heart and lungs are struggling
options.B: The patient is having a normal recovery
options.C: The patient is well hydrated and stable
options.D: The allergy medicine is working well

explanation: Tachycardia and desaturation reflect compensatory stress and failing respiratory function. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T4#GNS215_U5_T4_h6)

question: Which drug is given first to treat sudden, severe anaphylaxis?
explanation: Epinephrine is the essential first-line drug that reverses airway constriction and vascular collapse. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T4#GNS215_U5_T4_h7)

question: Why is emergency epinephrine given into the thigh muscle instead of under the skin?

options.A: The thigh muscle has fewer nerve endings
options.B: Injections under the skin destroy muscle tissue
options.C: It is less painful for adults
options.D: It enters the bloodstream much faster from muscle

explanation: Intramuscular injection into the vastus lateralis ensures rapid systemic absorption during emergencies. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T4#GNS215_U5_T4_h7)

question: Which detail is NOT needed when writing an incident report for an acute drug reaction?

options.A: The exact time the symptoms started
options.B: The patient's home address and phone number
options.C: The exact name of the drug that caused the reaction

explanation: Clinical documentation focuses on the incident specifics rather than demographic contact details. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T4#GNS215_U5_T4_h8)

question: Why do healthcare systems track and report adverse drug reactions?

options.A: To calculate hospital revenue and pharmacy stock
options.B: To punish nurses who make mistakes
options.C: To decide standard ward accommodation fees
options.D: To monitor drug safety trends across different hospitals

explanation: Pharmacovigilance reporting helps national bodies track adverse drug patterns and protect public health. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T4#GNS215_U5_T4_h8)
